title: Infra GPU Fleet, Capacity, CI/CD & IaC Runbook (2026 addendum)
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document is an operational addendum covering: GPU fleet capacity targets, cloud accounts & networking constraints relevant to GPU provisioning, recommended Terraform/IaC module patterns, CI/CD build and deployment flows for infra modules, and runbook procedures for capacity incidents. It consolidates guidance and concrete configurations we use at Redwood Inference in 2026 and is intended for infra engineers, SRE, and platform owners.

Goals

- Provide deterministic, tested IaC patterns for GPU provisioning and networking that minimize blast radius.
- Ensure capacity planning aligns with cost targets and latency SLOs for our serving clusters.
- Standardize CI/CD gating for infra modules and automated tests to reduce deployment failures.
- Give clear, step-by-step runbook actions for capacity shortage incidents and cluster recoveries.

1) GPU Fleet & Capacity Strategy

Short summary:
- Primary GPU types: A100-80GB (train/dev proof-of-concept pools), A100-40GB (inference/backlog), H100-80GB (high-performance inference), and G12/G10 for lower-cost embedding workloads.
- Capacity tiers: reserved (Dedicated), flexible (burstable), spot (best-effort) with automated fallback routing at request level.
- Target headroom: maintain 25% spare capacity for Dedicated pools during business hours and 40% during weekly maintenance windows.

Capacity thresholds and SLOs (operational table):

| Component | Metric | Warning threshold | Critical threshold | Owner | Action (automated) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Dedicated GPU pool (prod) | Utilization (vGPU equivalent) | 70% | 90% | gpu-fleet-team | Auto-burst to reserved-burst pool; page on critical |
| Serving queue length | 95p latency (ms) | 400ms | 800ms | serving-runtime | Reroute to fallback model variant; enable batching relax |
| Preemptible/spot reclaim | Percentage reclaimed | 15% | 30% | infra-ops | Increase reserved capacity; rehydrate jobs from hot cache |

Capacity planning cadence:
- Weekly: 4-hour review of utilization dashboards, upcoming customer commits, and forecasted model launches.
- Monthly: Capacity forecast + procurement requests for Dedicated pools; include cost delta scenarios for 10/20/50% growth.
- Quarterly: Hardware refresh planning (H100 purchase windows).

Ownership:
- gpu-fleet-team: capacity model, autoscaling policies, alerting thresholds.
- eng-sre: incident response, runbooks, paging rules.
- serving-runtime: request-level fallback and batching policy implementation.

2) Cloud Accounts & Networking Constraints

Account hygiene:
- GPU clusters are provisioned in dedicated cloud project/account per region (e.g., prod-us-west1-gpu-1) to isolate quotas, billing, and IAM.
- A shared infra account holds terraform state and remote backends; admin roles limited to infra-ops and security.

Networking patterns:
- VPC per environment (prod/staging/dev) with subnet segmentation for GPU node pools, bastion hosts, and management plane.
- Use egress-only NAT gateways for nodes that need external artifact access; restrict public IPs on GPU nodes.
- Private Service Connect / VPC Peering for control-plane to customer VPCs in Private deployments.

Standard firewall rules (example):
- Allow: node -> registry/artifact storage (443), telemetry endpoints (TCP/UDP per agent docs), NTP (123).
- Deny: inbound 0.0.0.0/0 to node management ports (22, 2375, 5000).

Quotas and soft limits to monitor:
- GPU count quota (per region): alert at 75% of quota.
- IP allocation: ensure /22 or larger for large GPU clusters to avoid exhaustion.

3) Terraform / IaC Module Patterns and Examples

Module guidelines:
- Single responsibility: modules should manage one resource family (e.g., gpu_node_pool, gpu_networking, gpu_iam).
- Explicit inputs/outputs: no implicit values; require region, size, instance_type, taints, and labels.
- Versioned modules and changelogs: tag modules with semver and publish release notes in the module registry.
- State separation: cluster state vs. node-pool state in different backends to reduce lock contention.

Recommended module interface (example snippet):

```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source        = "git::ssh://git.internal/redwood/terraform-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.4.0"
  project       = var.project
  region        = var.region
  node_count    = var.node_count
  instance_type = var.instance_type
  taints        = { dedicated = true }
  labels        = { team = var.owner_team }
}
```

Best practices for node pools:
- Expose autoscaling min/max; prefer CPU-based and custom GPU-utilization metrics from the telemetry pipeline.
- Taint dedicated pools (e.g., "gpu-mode=dedicated:NoSchedule") and use tolerations on serving workloads.
- Rolling updates: use max_unavailable=1 for production pools to avoid mass eviction.

4) CI/CD & Build Pipelines for Infra Modules

Pipeline stages (recommended):
1. Pre-merge: terraform fmt, tflint, static checks, unit tests for helper scripts.
2. Merge request: run terraform plan in isolated ephemeral environment using the same backend namespace; post plan summary and diffs to MR.
3. Canary apply: automated apply to staging account with automated smoke tests (node creation, simple workload run, network connectivity).
4. Production apply: gated by approvals (owner, security), apply in windows (region-by-region), and automated post-apply verification.

CI details:
- Use ephemeral infra test accounts (short-lived projects) for plan validation.
- Secrets: use KMS-backed secrets in CI runner; never store cloud creds in repo.
- Rollback: automated rollback script that can revert to previous state file snapshot and reapply node-pool counts.

Sample GitLab/Github Actions job names:
- ci/terraform/lint
- ci/terraform/plan
- ci/terraform/validate-smoke
- cd/terraform/canary-apply
- cd/terraform/prod-apply

5) Runbooks: Capacity Shortage Incident (Playbook)

Detection:
- Alert: gpu-pool-utilization-critical (>=90% for 5m) or serving-95p-latency-critical.
- Pager: on-call infra-ops -> page eng-sre primary if cross-service impact.

Immediate steps (first 15 minutes):
1. Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty and set public incident channel (Slack #incident-gpu).
2. Check Dashboard: GPU utilization, cluster events (preemptions), pending pods, and queue lengths.
3. If preemption spike: escalate to cloud provider support and trigger fallback policy: change serving routing to fallback-models (via runtime feature flag).
4. If sustained high utilization due to traffic: temporarily scale up reserved-burst pool (increase node_count by +20%) using terraform apply to the reserved-burst workspace.

If Terraform apply is needed (safe quick apply):
- Use the prod reserved-burst workspace with pre-approved plan token.
- Run: terraform init; terraform workspace select prod-reserved-burst; terraform plan -var 'node_count=...'; terraform apply -auto-approve;

Post-incident (30-90 minutes):
- Run capacity postmortem checklist: identify root cause, whether autoscaler misconfiguration, sudden customer load, or preemptions.
- Update capacity forecast if growth is persistent.
- Revert temporary increases once utilization returns to normal.

6) Runbooks: Node Replace / Kernel Patch

Context: When a kernel or driver patch requires node replacement, follow the cautious rolling pattern below to avoid mass eviction of large KV caches used by serving runtime.

Steps:
1. Create a new node-pool with same instance_type + taints but with a new label (patch=2026-k1).
2. Drain old nodes one at a time with a 10-minute wait for eviction: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m
3. Verify serving runtime KV cache hit-rate stays within 5% of baseline after each node drain.
4. If cache hit-rate drops >5% or tail latency increases 10%, pause and rollback the drain.

7) Testing and Observability

Required monitoring (must be present for any GPU pool deploy):
- GPU utilization per card, per node (1m, 5m, 15m windows).
- Pod-level GPU allocation and request vs. actual metrics.
- Serving tail latencies (50/95/99) and queue depth.
- Node replace progress metrics and eviction counts.

Synthetic smoke tests (post-apply):
- Node topology validation script (checks taints/labels/allocations).
- Serving smoke test: run a small inference job that validates end-to-end latency and model output basic checks.

8) Documentation and Onboarding (team wiki practices)

- Keep module README with: inputs/outputs, example usage, supported providers, and migration notes.
- Tag PRs that change module interfaces with 'module-interface-change' label and require two reviewers (owner + eng-sre).
- Maintain a short runbook stub in the module repo for quick ops for that module.

Appendix: Quick CLI snippets and useful queries

- Check GPU utilization (example cloud CLI):
  gcloud compute instances list --filter=\"labels=role:gpu\" --format=\"table(name,zone,status,labels,guestAccelerators)\"

- Example Terraform plan approval flow (automation):
  1) CI posts plan to MR and stores plan artifact in secure bucket with lifecycle 7 days.
  2) Canary job picks plan artifact and applies to staging project.
  3) Once canary smoke tests pass, product/owner approval required for prod apply.
